source: Light and Color
White light holds all colors, and objects look colored by the light they reflect.
Students think a red filter adds red to light, rather than blocking the other colors.

Isaac Newton passed sunlight through a glass prism and saw it spread into a rainbow of colors, then used a second prism to combine them back into white. White light is a mix of all the colors of the visible spectrum. What color an object looks depends on which of those colors it reflects, absorbs or transmits.

An object's color is the color of the light it reflects into your eyes; it absorbs the rest. A colored filter transmits light of its own color and absorbs (blocks) the others. With no light of its color to reflect, an object looks black.

A red apple in white light absorbs most of the colors and reflects mostly red, so red light reaches your eye. Put the same apple under pure blue light: there is no red light to reflect, and it absorbs the blue, so it looks black. A white object reflects every color, so it takes on the color of whatever light shines on it.
A prism spreads white light into its colors, because each color bends by a slightly different amount.
Colored lights, filters and objects. Change the light and the filter and watch which colors get through.

A shirt under colored light

A red shirt reflects red and absorbs other colors.
There is no red light to reflect, and it absorbs the green.

Thinking a red filter adds red to the light, or "dyes" it. A filter can only take colors away: white light contains red already, and the filter blocks everything else. Check: a red filter in front of a blue light gives darkness, not purple.
